title: Idempotent kernel bootstrap and compile-time probe harness
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Problem: Our current kernel startup sequence performs a lot of late-binding symbol resolution and on-demand kernel registration which leads to non-deterministic cold-start variance across heterogeneous fleets (different OS distributions, driver versions, mixed vendor GPUs). This manifests as spiky tail latency and occasional CI canaries failing during scale tests.

Goal: Implement an idempotent, deterministic kernel bootstrap with a compile-time probe harness that emits a small, verifiable manifest at build-time. At runtime the agent will validate the manifest and either fast-path to an eager, prelinked kernel-init or switch to an instrumented lazy path with strict watchdogs. The overall goal is to reduce boot jitter, make kernel init repeatable across binary versions, and provide a safe rollback/fallback path when binary/driver mismatches are detected.

Scope: Modify the runtime bootstrap sequence; introduce a lightweight compile-time probe generator (go/ruby/python toolchain) that runs during packaging to snapshot symbol expectations, kernel dispatch table shapes, and a small set of microbench markers. Add runtime validation logic, a metrics export (bootstrap.success, bootstrap.rollback, bootstrap.latency_ms), and feature-flagged rollout control. This does not include changing Cutlass/Triton internals beyond build-time probes and symbol manifest generation.

Out-of-scope: Full binary grafting or delta patcher (separate initiative), and changing model-serving dispatching semantics.

Design overview:
1) Compile-time probe harness: a build step that links a tiny probe binary against the exact kernel artifact set and records resolved symbol addresses (or stable name hashes), required ABI shapes, and a small set of microbenchmarks (e.g., tiny GEMM run). The output is a JSON manifest embedded into the runtime package (signed by release key).
2) Idempotent bootstrap routine: at startup the runtime checks the manifest signature, replays a small deterministic probe to confirm the environment matches the recorded expectations, and if successful moves to the eager-init path that pre-resolves key symbol references and warms a bounded kernel cache. If validation fails, the runtime falls back to an instrumented lazy resolver that performs per-symbol resolution with strict timeouts and records telemetry for postmortem.
3) Rollback and safety: the runtime will persist a recent-good manifest and allow automatic rollback to previous manifests on repeated failures. A kill-switch feature flag exposes the lazy-path-only behavior for rapid rollbacks.
acceptance_criteria: Deterministic bootstrap reduces 95th/99th percentile init latency variance by >= 50% on mixed fleet tests
Runtime exposes metrics: bootstrap.success, bootstrap.rollback.count, bootstrap.latency_ms
Signed manifest verification implemented and tested in CI; corrupted manifests trigger safe fallback
Canary deployment runs for 72h without bootstrap regressions on dedicated canary fleet
Documentation updated: build step, manifest format, operator runbooks
test_plan: Unit tests for manifest generation and signature verification
CI job that builds probe manifest for current build matrix (CUDA 11/12/13, Triton variants) and verifies it can be validated by the runtime image
Stress test: 2k simultaneous cold starts on heterogeneous nodes comparing baseline vs new bootstrap (automation script in infra/tests/bootstrap_stress.sh)
Chaos test: introduce a driver-level mismatch on a subset of nodes and assert that runtime falls back to lazy-resolver and records appropriate telemetry
Performance microbench: confirm microbenchmark numbers embedded in manifest are within expected thresholds or mark for manual review
rollout_plan: Stage 1: deploy to internal dev fleet with flag enabled (1 day)
Stage 2: enable on canary fleet (5% of production) for 72 hours with increased telemetry retention
Stage 3: progressively increase to 25% then 100% if no regressions and bootstrap.rollback rate < 0.1%
Rollback: flip feature flag off or revert to previous signed-manifest artifact if bootstrap.rollback spikes > 1% over 1h
notes: Decision: use signed JSON manifest to avoid requiring heavy cryptographic infra; signing will use existing CI release keypair
Trade-off: eager prelinking reduces jitter but increases resident memory and binary warm-up time; limited prelink set to top-10 hot symbols to balance
Alternative evaluated: fully lazy resolution with aggressive prefetch from warmup daemon - rejected because it did not eliminate early tail latency in stress tests
Compatibility: manifest format is versioned (v1) to allow staged schema changes; runtime will accept older manifests with a compatibility shim
Interop: coordinate with releases team to add probe step to package pipeline (see CONFLUENCE doc)
